chapters.label: Every pupil, and making it last

scenes.narration: In my last school, every teacher taught computing their own way, from scratch. Pupils met loops three times and functions never. A scheme of work fixed that in one term.
Today: a scheme of work for computing, from the first grades to the last.
A scheme of work is the plan for a subject across the year: which units, in what order, how long each takes, and how you’ll know pupils learned. It turns good lessons into a path pupils can climb.

Plan the progression across grades. The youngest work unplugged and with the robot’s cards. Then come blocks and very short programs. Then real Python: variables, decisions, loops, lists and functions. Each stage builds on the last.

For one term, plan four to six units of three or four lessons each. Give every unit one big idea, an unplugged start, a plugged part and a small project. Put an assessment point at the end of each unit: a short quiz, a Parsons task, or a program.

With few devices, plan who gets them and when. A simple timetable shares the school’s phones or tablets between classes. Unplugged and paper lessons fill the other weeks, so no class waits a whole term to touch a device.
Quick check! You’re planning computing for nine- and ten-year-olds who have never programmed. Which unit should come first?

Algorithms and loops, with the robot. Each later unit needs the ones before it: you can’t teach lists before loops, or functions before variables. Draw the progression as a ladder before you write a single lesson.

Make the scheme work for everyone. Plan paper versions of every task for pupils without devices at home. Watch that girls and quieter pupils get turns as driver, not only as reporter. And pick examples from your pupils’ own lives.

Plans fail when one enthusiast leaves. Share the scheme in a folder everyone can find. Train one colleague each term, and start a computing club where pupils help each other. Then computing outlives any one teacher.

In the app, open Sorting race, as one unit of your scheme might use it. Start unplugged with pupils sorting cards, then run the race on one phone: eight bars, then thirty-two. Ask the class which algorithm they’d choose, and why.
Your turn. You lead computing, and you’re moving to another school next year. What best keeps computing going?

scenes.on_screen_text: A ladder · progression · big ideas · last
scenes.narration: Share it and train others. Remember: a scheme of work is a ladder of units. Progress from unplugged and the robot, to blocks, to Python. Give each unit one big idea and an assessment point. Share devices fairly, and make it last.

Try it with your colleagues: draft one term of computing on a single page. List four to six units, the big idea of each, and how you’ll assess it. Share it, and ask one colleague to teach a unit with you.

checkpoints.prompt: Planning for nine- and ten-year-olds who have never programmed: which unit comes first?

options.text: Algorithms and loops with the robot, unplugged

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — start with exact instructions and loops, unplugged and with the robot; Python comes later.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — young beginners start with algorithms and loops, unplugged; functions and algorithm speed come years later.

checkpoints.prompt: You lead computing and move schools next year. What best keeps it going?

options.text: Keep the plans on your own phone
A shared scheme, trained colleagues and a club
Teach extra lessons before you leave

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — shared plans and trained colleagues mean computing doesn’t depend on one person.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a scheme in one person’s hands leaves with them. Share it and train others.
